div.p: The responsiveness of autonomous driving (AD) systems is highly important for safety and performance of the vehicles. It is defined as end-to-end latency from sensing the surrounding environment to executing control signals, which determines how quickly the vehicle changes the driving behavior in response to an external event. The AD software stacks are modeled as a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of multi-rate tasks with variable execution times, where the probabilistic end-toend latencies (PEELs) of multiple task sequences need to be minimized on a multi-core processor. This paper proposes a novel schedule synthesis that reduces the PEELs of task sequences of interest under multi-core partitioned EDF scheduling. In the first stage, we generate a baseline schedule to avoid non-usable idle intervals as much as possible by estimating a lower bound on the total non-usable idle time. A non-usable idle interval is an idle interval that cannot be utilized by tasks preceding the interval, thus worsening the graph schedulability. In the second stage, we formulate the problem of reducing the PEELs of multiple task sequences under the baseline schedule into a multi-objective optimization of task phases and search for an optimal phase combination. Through experiments with a real AD stack called Autoware as well as synthetic task graphs, we show that our synthesis significantly improves the graph schedulability and the resulting end-to-end tail latencies.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: The responsiveness of autonomous driving (AD) systems is highly important for safety and performance of the vehicles. It is defined as end-to-end latency from sensing the surrounding environment to executing control signals, which determines how quickly the vehicle changes the driving behavior in response to an external event. For example, if the end-to-end latency is 200 ms between sensing a pedestrian in front and executing an emergency stop signal, a vehicle driving at 108 km/h (= 30 m/s) will run towards the pedestrian by six meters without any proper control. Thus, for the AD software stack, it is necessary to minimize the latencies in generating a processor schedule.

Recently, in the real-time research community, there has been much progress in analyzing the end-to-end latency of cyber-physical systems. The relevant works can be categorized into deterministic and probabilistic analyses with a graph of tasks. Deterministic analyses [1]- [8] compute the worst-case response times (WCRT) of tasks or the worst-case end-toend latency over a sequence of tasks, given the worst-case execution times (WCET) of the tasks. Probabilistic analyses [9]- [13] give probabilistic versions of WCET, WCRT, and end-to-end latencies, given the variable task execution times. In the cost-competitive automotive industry, however, the probabilistic ones are much preferred because they do not over-provision the processor resources against the worst-case demands of tasks, thus leading to a lower cost of system implementation. Recently, for AD systems, a probabilistic analysis called PEELA [13] has been proposed to compute the probabilistic end-to-end latencies (PEELs) of all possible task sequences found in the graph. The analysis provides a probabilistic guarantee that the analyzed distribution of the end-to-end latency L(S) for each sequence S upperbounds the observed one from a real vehicle for S, in that Prob(L(S) observed ≤ t) ≥ Prob(L(S) analyzed ≤ t) for any t ≥ 0. From this guarantee, it gives a safe tail latency of any percentile, e.g., 99.9th, for each task sequence.

In the paper, we propose a novel schedule synthesis to reduce the PEELs of task sequences of interest under multi-core partitioned EDF scheduling while modeling the AD software stack as a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of multi-rate tasks with variable execution times. The proposed synthesis consists of two stages: (1) baseline schedule generation and (2) task phases optimization. In the first stage, a scheduling heuristic creates a baseline schedule on a multi-core processor which defines a task-to-core mapping with per-core task priority orders for each subgraph of tasks with the same period. The resulting schedule is called a baseline because the task priority order on each core will not be changed in the second stage. In the baseline scheduling, we deal with a problem called non-usable idle intervals, which may occur within a subgraph and worsen the schedulability of the entire graph. A non-usable idle interval is an idle interval that cannot be utilized by tasks preceding the interval no matter how long they execute, thus has an effect of increasing the average utilization of the underlying core. An increase in the average core utilization may lead to an increase in the end-to-end latency of each task sequence visiting the core, thus possibly degrades the schedulability of the given DAG [13]. Thus, in order to generate a baseline schedule with as little non-usable idle intervals as possible, we present a systematic method to compute a lower bound on the total average non-usable idle time for each core. Combined with this method, traditional heuristics [15] used for DAG scheduling in the deterministic domain can be adopted with little modification while reducing occurrences of the intervals. Moreover, we also propose a new DAG scheduler that always guarantees no occurrences of nonusable idle intervals.

In the second stage, with the baseline schedule generated, a multi-objective optimizer coordinates all task phases in the entire graph so that the PEELs of interest can be reduced. In the task phases optimization, we formulate the problem of reducing end-to-end tail latencies of multiple task sequences into multi-objective optimization and find a Pareto-optimal combination of task phases by applying an evolutionary algorithm. In our case, a Pareto-optimal combination means that, under the baseline schedule, a change of a task phase in the combination leading to an improvement of the tail latency of one task sequence necessarily results in a degradation of another. To evaluate the proposed synthesis, we perform experiments on a task graph used in a real AD stack called Autoware [14] and a set of synthetic task graphs. For validation purposes, we instrument Autoware to realize the schedules generated by the proposed synthesis. The experiments show that our proposed baseline schedulers effectively suppress the increase in the average core utilizations, and that the task phases optimization further reduces the end-to-end tail latency by up to 13.0% for synthetic task graphs.
The contributions of the paper can be summarized as follows:
• To the best of our knowledge, it is the first attempt to generate a holistic multi-core schedule for a real AD stack that provides a probabilistic guarantee on the end-to-end latencies.

• The proposed synthesis provides a systematic method to compute a lower bound on the total average nonusable idle time, which allows to apply any of traditional list-based DAG scheduling algorithms with deterministic execution times to the probabilistic domain. • The Autoware stack is extended to incorporate the assumptions of the proposed synthesis, which makes it possible for the Autoware to provide a probabilistic guarantee on the end-to-end latencies. The organization of the paper is as follows. In Section II, we describe the system model and summarize the PEELA, and in Section III, we explain the proposed synthesis in detail. In Section IV, the experimental results are given, and in Section V, the related work is reviewed. Finally, in Section VI, we conclude the paper with future research directions.

div.head: II. PRELIMINARIES A. System model and problem formulation
div.p: The system model we assume is the same as the one in the PEELA. That is, the system consists of a multi-core processor and executes an AD stack, which is modeled as a DAG of tasks communicating with messages. If a task τ i directly sends a message to τ j , τ i is an immediate predecessor of τ j , and τ j is an immediate successor of τ i , denoted by τ i → τ j . If a task τ j is reachable from τ i through a direct path in the graph, τ i is a predecessor of τ j , and τ j is a successor of τ i . The entire graph Γ consists of a set of K disjoint subgraphs, Γ = {Γ 1 , • • • , Γ K }, each of which is composed of tasks periodically released with the same period as the subgraph period T k . Each subgraph Γ k is formally defined as (T k , ϕ k , V k , E k ) where T k is the period of Γ k , ϕ k is the graph phase, which is a relative offset of the release time of (the first released task within) the subgraph Γ k to a reference time origin (0 ≤ ϕ k < T k ), V k is the set of tasks defined as the vertices in Γ k , i.e., {τ k 1 , • • • , τ k nk }, and E k is the set of directed edges between the tasks. Each task

For the task graph, the following assumptions are made in the PEELA.

A1. Each task reads messages as soon as it starts execution, not in the middle, and sends a message to the successors right before it finishes execution. A2. For a task to become runnable, it should receive a message from every immediate predecessor in the same subgraph (i.e., blocking I/O mode) while it does not have to do from any task in a different subgraph (i.e., nonblocking I/O mode). Every source task becomes runnable as soon as it releases. A3. For any directed sequence of subgraphs along which messages flow, i.e., Γ 1 → Γ 2 → • • • → Γ L found in the entire graph, the involved subgraphs have a nonincreasing order of periods, i.e.,

No input message is dropped in a task to generate the corresponding output message. A5. Each subgraph is assigned a dedicated set of CPU cores while every task in the subgraph is statically pinned to a certain core in the set. Two or more subgraphs cannot share the same CPU core. A6. Every core is scheduled by EDF independently of the other cores.

Assumption A1 is safe in that it makes the analysis safe even for task graphs that do not satisfy it. The assumptions of the blocking intra-graph communication (A2) and the increasingly shortened periods of subgraph sequences (A3) make at most one input message outstanding for every communication channel in each task. Assumption A4 makes it possible to maintain one-to-one correspondence from a sensor message to a control message, thus the end-to-end latency can be defined for every sensor message. The assumptions of the non-blocking intergraph communication (A2) and the multi-core partitioned scheduling (A5) build an isolated execution environment for every subgraph. That is, the timing behavior of a subgraph is not affected by others. According to assumptions A5 and A6, all the tasks assigned to the same core are likely to be scheduled in FCFS (First Come First Served) by EDF. However, there is the possibility that preemptions may occur according to the task dependencies. For details, refer to Figure 3 in [13]. Note that we do not deal with how to distribute a fixed number of cores to the subgraphs in the paper.

Under the above assumptions, it is proved in [13] that the PEELA gives a safe end-to-end latency distribution for every task sequence in Γ. For the jth instance S j of task sequence S, the end-to-end latency L(S j ) is defined as the difference between the release of the jth instance τ f,j of the first task τ f in S and the completion of an instance τ l,k of the last task τ l in S, that reacts to the message generated by τ f,j . Then, the end-to-end latency L(S) of S is defined as a random variable describing the latency values of all possible instances of S. Note that L(S) is not merely the sum of the execution times of all the tasks involved in the sequence, but may include an idle interval caused by a task's waiting on some of the input channels in the blocking mode. The analyzed latency distribution by the PEELA is said to be safe because it upperbounds the observed distribution from a real vehicle in that Prob(L(S) observed ≤ t) ≥ Prob(L(S) analyzed ≤ t) for any t ≥ 0 under the assumption of independent task execution times. Even for the cases where the maximum utilization U max exceeds 1.0 for some core(s), the PEELA can give a limiting distribution of L(S <h> j ) by approaching the hyperperiod index h → ∞, as long as the average core utilization U is less than 1.0 for every core in general. A hyperperiod is a duration whose length is equal to the least common multiple of all subgraph periods, i.e., T 1 , T 2 , • • • , and T K .

In the paper, our goal is to find a multi-core schedule such that the c-percentile tail latency T L c (S) of each task sequence S of interest can be less than a threshold T L * (S) associated with S. A graph is said to be schedulable with a multi-core schedule if T L(S) ≤ T L * (S) for every S of interest. The schedule is defined as the task-to-core assignment a's, the graph phases ϕ's, and the task phases φ's. For the sake of simplicity, we define the absolute phase

div.head: III. PROPOSED SYNTHESIS
div.p: The goal of the proposed synthesis is to generate a multicore schedule such that the tail latency T L(S) of each S of interest in Γ can be less than or equal to a given threshold T L * (S). To this end, the proposed synthesis performs two stages: (1) baseline schedule generation and (2) task phases optimization. In the following, we first investigate into the problem of non-usable idle intervals in generating a baseline schedule.

div.head: A. Non-usable idle intervals
div.p: For baseline schedule generation, we consider traditional list-based DAG scheduling used in the deterministic domain [15]. However, a naive application of the traditional scheduling may cause a problem called non-usable idle intervals, which have an effect of increasing the average utilization U core of the associated core. According to [13], as U core of each core approaches to 1.0, the end-to-end tail latencies of task sequences on a multi-core system get longer and longer, thus the graph schedulability may be degraded. In the following, U core only denotes the nominal average core utilization, which equals the sum of the average utilizations of tasks assigned to the core, and U core denotes the effective average core utilization that adds the effect of the intervals to U core . To help understand why the intervals matter, let us apply a traditional scheduler to Γ 1 in Figure 1 with the new task parameters shown in Table II.

A list-based DAG scheduling performs as follows. It first computes a priority for every task in the DAG, which is used in task assignment, not task execution, and makes a ready list of the tasks in a descending order of the priorities. Then, it assigns the first task in the list to a core that allows the earliest execution by appending the task to a list of the assigned tasks to the core. This assignment will be repeated until the ready list becomes empty. One such scheduler is HLFET (Highest bottom Level First with Estimated execution Times). For HLFET, the priority of each task is the bottom level of the task, which is defined as the length of the longest path from the task to the sink task of the graph. That is, the bottom level equals the sum of the estimated execution times of all the tasks on the path. In the deterministic domain, as the estimated execution time, the worst-case execution time is used in most cases. However, in our domain, we choose the average execution time C as the estimated one because we want to distribute the tasks to the cores in terms of the average load. Thus, for Γ 1 , the bottom levels are computed as follows:
div.formula: btmlevel(τ D ) = C D = 1.5, btmlevel(τ C ) = C C + C D = 3.5 + 1.5 = 5, btmlevel(τ B ) = C B + C D = 1.5 + 1.5 = 3, and btmlevel(τ A ) = C A + C C + C D = 1.5 + 3.5 + 1.5 = 6.5.

div.head: B. Computation of Effective Core Utilization U core
div.p: To generate a baseline schedule with better schedulability, we need to check if the intermediate schedule being constructed may cause a non-usable idle interval for each task assignment. In this subsection, we will describe how to identify such intervals in an arbitrary DAG schedule and estimate a lower bound NT lb core on the total average NT for each core. The reason why we compute NT lb core is that a graph schedule may be too complex to analyze the exact average NT due to multiple non-usable intervals possibly overlapping each other and due to an infinite number of combinations of the variable task execution times. Each time a task is assigned to a core, our baseline scheduler will assign the task to a core giving a lowest U lb core with the task. U lb core is defined as
div.formula: U core + 1 T NT lb core .
div.p: Even if the exact average NT may not be computed, our experiments will show that the baseline scheduler using U lb core generates better schedules than with U core in most cases.

div.head: C. Baseline Schedule Generation
div.p: To reduce the end-to-end tail latencies, we need to generate a good baseline schedule for a given task graph. To this aim, we generate a baseline schedule for each of the subgraphs and simply merge the resulting subgraph schedules into one as the baseline schedule for the entire graph. This is possible because the subgraph schedules do not share any core due to the assumption of partitioned scheduling. As baseline schedulers, we propose two DAG schedulers: HLFETNT and BLFLT. HLFETNT (Highest bottom Level First with Estimated execution Times and Non-usable idle Times) is our variant of Our experiments will show that HLFETNT is better for graphs leading to low average core utilizations while BLFLT is better for graphs leading to high average core utilizations.

The two proposed baseline schedulers take different approaches to balancing the loads of cores. HLFETNT distributes tasks across the given set of cores while BLFLT clusters tasks on a one-core-by-one-core basis. To compare HLFETNT and BLFLT, let us consider a subgraph example in Figure 7. In this example, there is a graph of five tasks with the same C = 1, and the bottom levels of the tasks are as follows: btmlevel(τ A ) = btmlevel(τ B ) = 3, btmlevel(τ C ) = btmlevel(τ D ) = 2, and btmlevel(τ E ) = 1. In this case, the BFS level of each task, bf slevel, assuming to take the dummy Ω as the source task, happens to be equal to the btmlevel.

Then, as described earlier, HLFETNT distributes the tasks on the given cores by assigning a task with the highest btmlevel to a core with the lowest U in every task assignment. The resulting schedule is shown in the left box in Figure 7. In this simple example, no NT happens to occur (even if we use HLFET). Thus, the resulting average makespan of the schedule is 3. On the contrary, BLFLT clusters the tasks on a one-core-by-one-core basis by assigning a task with the highest bf slevel to the current core as long as the resulting U core does not exceed a certain threshold U T H . This threshold
div.formula: U T H is determined to be 1 T × max( i Ci m , max i C i ), where i Ci m
div.p: is the ideal average load for each of the given m cores, and the ceiling is taken because the probability distributions are defined in integer domain. The reason why we consider max i C i is that we have to allow at least one core to contain the task with the largest C, possibly greater than the ideal average load. Thus, the load threshold computed for the above example, not divided by T , is max( 52 , 1) = 3. The resulting schedule is shown in the right box in Figure 7, which gives the average makespan of 4.

From the above example, we observe that HLFETNT performs better than BLFLT in terms of the average makespan. This is because HLFETNT tends to better exploit task-level parallelism while BLFLT tends to exploit pipeline parallelism, not task-level parallelism. Nonetheless, for the cases where HLFETNT suffers from a high U due to non-avoidable NTs, BLFLT may perform better.

div.head: D. Task Phases Optimization
div.p: Once the baseline schedule of the entire graph is constructed, we conduct task phases optimization in terms of the absolute task phases Φ to further reduce the end-toend latency of each task sequence. However, since there are multiple task paths of interest that share the same task(s), a task phase combination may be advantageous to one sequence, but disadvantageous to others at the same time. For example, let us consider two paths, S 1 = τ A → τ B → τ C and S 2 = τ A → τ C within a subgraph, assuming that τ A , τ B , and τ C have a constant execution time of 1 and a period of 3, and that τ A and τ B are assigned to core 1 while τ C is assigned to core 2. In this example, it is clear that, to achieve a minimum value of 3 for T L(S 1 ), it is required that Φ A = 0, Φ B = 1, and Φ C = 2, which leads to T L(S 2 ) = 3. On the contrary, to achieve a minimum value of 2 for T L(S 2 ), if we set Φ A = 0 and Φ B = Φ C = 1, it leads to T L(S 1 ) = 5 because every instance of S 1 starts from τ A,j in the jthe period and ends at τ C,j+1 in the (j + 1)th period. This trade-off relation may happen even across subgraphs. An argument vector, e.g., Φ, that leads to an improvement of one objective function, e.g., T L(S 1 ) or T L(S 2 ), but necessarily requires a degradation of another is said to be a Pareto-optimal solution. In this case, we need to search for a solution space called a Pareto frontier by formulating the problem into multi-objective optimization. That is, T L(S p ) of each S p of interest is treated as an objective function
div.formula: T L Sp of (Φ 1 , • • • , Φ N ) where p = 1, • • • , P (P = the number of paths). argmin (Φ1,••• ,ΦN ) T L Sp (Φ 1 , • • • , Φ N ) p = 1, • • • , P subject to Φ 1 = 0 0 ≤ Φ i ≤ T i -1 i = 2, • • • , N Φ k i ≤ Φ k j for any τ k i ⇒ τ k j
div.p: In the above formulation, Φ 1 = 0 because we use τ 1 as an anchor task, and vary the phases of the other tasks. The constraint that 0 ≤ Φ i ≤ T i -1 is added since every task is periodic. The constraint that Φ k i ≤ Φ k j represents the precedence relation between any two tasks in the same subgraph, i.e., τ k i → τ k j or τ k i ⇒ τ k j . Then, to search for Pareto-optimal solutions, we use an evoluationary algorithm called NSGA-II (Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm-II) [17]. This algorithm starts with an initial population of M argument vectors, creates their offspring, consisting of M children, thus leading to a combined population of M parents and M children. Then, it evaluates each of the 2M argument vectors in terms of P objective functions and sorts them considering the dominating relations among the vectors according to the evaluation result. Finally, it takes only the first M best vectors from the sorted ones as new parents while dropping the remaining vectors, and goes back to creating their offspring in order to repeat the entire process. This process should be repeated in order to achieve a good spread of Pareto-optimal solutions. Once the solutions are obtained, we may select a particular solution of interest by comparing a weighted sum of the resulting values of the objective functions. In our experiments, we will set all the weights to one, which means that all the task paths of interest are equally important.

The time complexity of a single iteration of NSGA-II is O(P M 2 + AM ) where O(P M 2 ) is the sorting complexity [17] and O(AM ) is the analysis complexity with M different argument vectors and the PEELA's analysis time of A. If the required number of iterations is G, the resulting synthesis complexity is O(GP M 2 + GAM ). According to [13], the analysis time is dominated by the maximum of U core 's in the given schedule. In our experiments, with the computer described in Section IV-B, the task phases optimization with NSGA-II requires 166 seconds for a synthetic graph of 30

div.head: IV. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS
div.p: To evaluate the proposed synthesis, we have written two programs in Python: (1) schedule synthesizer and (2) PEELAnalyzer. Given a task graph, the schedule synthesizer generates a multi-core schedule using a baseline scheduler with or without the task phases optimization, which is implemented with the NSGA-II solver in pymoo [18]. Then, the PEELAnalyzer takes both the graph and the generated schedule to compute the T L(S) for every S of interest. Following [13], the analyzer implements the whole probabilistic end-to-end latency analysis, which covers both harmonic and non-harmonic subgraphs.

div.head: A. Evaluation with synthetic task graphs
div.p: For the experiments, we randomly generate 100 task graphs, each consisting of 30 tasks. The 30 tasks are randomly distributed to four subgraphs, Γ100, Γ40, Γ25, and Γ10 with T = 100, 40, 25, and 10, respectively, according to Stafford's randfixedsum algorithm [20]. Every subgraph Γ k in Γ has the same average utilization U Γ , a portion of which is also randomly distributed to the constituent tasks according to the randfixedsum. In the experiments, U Γ is varied from 0.8 to 1.2, which has the effect of varying U core when a fixed number of cores is dedicated to each subgraph. Each task τ k i has a uniform execution time distribution with an average equal to

div.p: To determine the shape of a subgraph, we use the shape parameter α introduced in [19]. It defines the height and width of the subgraph, where the height denotes the number of levels and the width denotes the number of tasks at each level in the subgraph. A small value of α 1.0 produces a thin graph with a low degree of task parallelism while a large value of α 1.0 produces a fat graph with a high degree of parallelism. α is varied from 0.5 to 2.0. Each task has 1.5 edges on average to the successor tasks.

For each graph Γ, we first generate baseline schedules for three schedulers, HLFET, HLFETNT, and BLFLT, and then apply the in-phase condition to the schedules, which means that every task has the same zero phase. In the baseline schedule generation, the same number of cores, which is four, are assumed to be dedicated to each subgraph in every graph. To evaluate the schedulability of the resulting baseline schedules, we measure the effective average subgraph utilization U (Γ) of each subgraph, defined as the sum of U core 's of the dedicated cores to the subgraph, and take U (Γ) = max( U (Γ100), U (Γ40), U (Γ25), U (Γ10)) as the effective average graph utilization of the entire graph Γ in order to see the influences of the NTs.

Figure 8(a) shows the number of task graphs determined to be analyzable among the 100 synthetic graphs. We determine a graph to be analyzable (TBA) if every core in the resulting schedule has U core ≤ 0.7. The case of U core > 0.7 means that U max core > 1.4, which may significantly degrade the response times of the tasks mapped on the core, and in turn, the endto-end tail latencies of task paths visiting the core. Even if the ideal U core is just 0.25 with four cores in the case of U Γ = 1.0, such cases may happen since no baseline scheduler can always achieve the ideal balancing due to the non-uniform average task execution times. From the figure, in the case of HLFET, as U Γ is varied from 0.8 to 1.2, the number of the TBA task graphs with α = 0.5 largely decreases from 85 (U Γ =0.8) to 18 (U Γ =1.2). However, this tendency is significantly mitigated in HLFETNT, thus the number of TBA graphs with α = 0.5 starts from 100 (U Γ =0.8) and decreases to 61 (U Γ =1.2), which is much better than HLFET. Nonetheless, note that HLFETNT does not completely remove NTs. Only BLFLT produces NT-free schedules for all the 100 synthetic graphs regardless of α. Figure 8(b) shows U (Γ) for the same 100 synthetic graphs. From the figure, it is obvious that a small α and/or a high U Γ lead to high U (Γ)'s for HLFET. When α = 0.5 and U Γ = 1.2, the average U (Γ) of the 100 graphs amounts to 2.18 for HLFET, but 1.31 for HLFETNT, and 1.2 for BLFLT.

For only TBA graph Γ's obtained in Figure 8(a), we apply the PEELA to get the average of the AT L's of all the TBA graphs with or without the task phases optimization for HLFET, HLFETNT, and BLFLT. The AT L is the average of the end-to-end tail latencies of 99.9999th percentile for all task paths of interest, which are analyzed by the PEELA. From the figure, we can see that, for various α and U Γ , the average AT L of the in-phase HLFETNT schedules is very close to that of HLFET in most cases. However, in the case where α = 0.5 and U Γ = 1.2, the average AT L for HLFET is 289, which is worse than that of HLFETNT, 268.39. div.head: B. Case study with Autoware
div.p: In this subsection, we perform a case study with Autoware. Since Autoware is a real AD stack, we run it with a vehicle simulator called SVL [21] with two virtual Lidars (one for the front and the other for the rear) and one front camera. From a 5 minute-long simulation run, we obtain a sensor recording file which captures the surrounding environment in a virtual street in the simulator and then run Autoware while replaying the file in real-time. The computing system is equipped with an Intel i7 processor with 6 cores (12 virtual cores) operating at 2.6 GHz, main memory of 32 GB, and a GPU of RTX 2070. It runs Ubuntu Linux 20.04, ROS2 Galactic version, and Autoware.auto v1.0.0. Figure 10 shows the task graph of the Autoware, which consists of three subgraphs: control subgraph with T = 10, vision subgraph with T = 50, and Lidar subgraph with T = 100ms. The Autoware stack is instrumented to collect timing information such as task Fig. 10. The task graph of Autoware execution times and end-to-end latencies in the same way as in [13]. The task execution times are collected while executing the Autoware graph five times with the same recording file. With the collected task ETDs, we use the proposed synthesis to generate HLFET, HLFETNT and BLFLT schedules with four cores: one for the control subgraph, two for the Lidar subgraph, and one for the vision subgraph. Table V gives the task assignment results of the three schedulers. From the table, we can see that, for the Autoware graph, HLFET happens to generate the same result as HLFETNT, and that BLFLT does not well balance the load between core 1 and 2 due to the greedy assignment to fill the load threshold for core 1, which could be improved with more combinatorial search. Then, to collect the end-to-end latencies of task paths, we execute the Autoware graph five times under the in-phase combination and also under the optimized phase combination by the proposed multi-objective optimization. The paths of interest are {F |R}LD → EU C → MOT → BHP → P P S, two Lidar-based detection-to-control paths, and {F |R}LD → NDT → EKF → P P S, two Lidar-based localization-tocontrol paths. The five latency histograms obtained for each path are averaged into one distribution, from which the tail latency of 99.9999th percentile is extracted.

Table VI gives the TLs obtained for each task path under the three schedules. Each column of the table gives two numbers: one without parentheses and the other with parentheses. The former is the one directly measured with the instrumented Autoware being executed while the latter is the one analyzed with the PEELA. From the table, it is clear that the optimized phase combination gives better latencies. Moreover, it confirms that the measured TL ≤ the analyzed TL for each path, which is a probabilistic guarantee provided by the PEELA. The TL of F LD → MOT → P P S is decreased under HLFETNT from 101 to 76ms (25% improvement), while that is decreased under BLFLT from 104 to 93ms (10.6% improvement).

div.head: V. RELATED WORK
div.p: In real-time domain, there are several studies that analyze the timing behavior of graph-structured software. They can be classified in the task model they use. One group of the studies [7], [8], [12] deals with a graph of single-rate subtasks. For example, the schedulability analysis proposed in [12] deals with a single graph of subtasks with variable execution times and the same period under EDF scheduling on a uniprocessor system. This analysis is a probabilistic extension of the deterministic schedulability analysis, presented in [25], and provides a safe schedulability test by transforming both task release times and deadlines into probability distributions. As another example, the parallel DAG scheduling is presented in [7] to exploit the nested parallelism in the OpenMP task and to derive the response time bound under a hierarchical scheduling. Also, the WCRT analysis [8] deals with OpenMP programs with loop structures, which create a directed cyclic graph.

Another group of the studies [3]- [6], [11] addresses multiple independent tasks possibly with different periods, each task modeled as a graph of subtasks with the same period. For example, the probabilistic schedulability analysis (PSA) proposed in [11] analyzes a set of multiple DAGs found in a drone system under fixed-priority scheduling on a multi-core system. In each DAG, an end-to-end latency is probabilistically computed between a source and a sink subtask within a task, assuming that all the subtasks within the DAG release at the same time. Based on the PSA, a synthesis method that determines subtask-level priorities is also presented in [11]. For a set of multiple DAGs with the worst-case subtask execution times, a multi-core partitioning heuristic exploiting the subtask-level parallelism is also proposed in [26].

However, the above two task models are not general enough to cover the AD stacks, which consist of a graph of multirate tasks (or subgraphs). This task model is addressed by the other group [1], [13]. The PEELA [13] uses this model to analyze the end-to-end latency distributions of task paths across the subgraphs. The deterministic analysis proposed in [1] also analyzes the worst-case end-to-end latency across the subgraphs for a ROS2-based robotic system. However, since the analysis is deterministic, it cannot deal with the task graphs used in the paper, which allow U core to exceed 1.0 for some core(s).

In the vehicle domain, there are several studies to analyze, evaluate and improve the timing behavior of the AD stacks. The probabilistic analysis presented in [9] derives a safe probabilistic WCET (pWCET) for each of the tasks composing the Apollo stack [22] using a theory called Extreme Value Theory. In [14], the Autoware stack is evaluated in terms of average end-to-end latencies on an automotive embedded board called NVIDIA Drive PX2. In [23], an extended version of laxity-based scheduling on a multi-core system is proposed to improve the worst-case latency of task sequences. In [24], a resource management method is presented to smooth peak memory demands of software pipelines found in Autoware in order to reduce the worst-case delays.

div.head: VI. CONCLUSION
div.p: In the paper, we have proposed a novel schedule synthesis for task graphs from autonomous driving systems. The proposed synthesis deals with the problem of non-usable idle intervals, which arises in the probabilistic domain. It consists of baseline schedule generation and task phases optimization. In the baseline schedule generation, the two proposed schedulers called HLFETNT and BLFLT successfully suppress the occurrences of non-usable idle times, thus significantly improve the schedulability of given task graphs. In the task phases optimization, an optimal combination of task phases is found that reduces end-to-end tail latencies of task paths of interest. The experiments have shown that the two schedulers significantly improve the graph schedulability, and that the task phases optimization further improves the end-to-end tail latency by up to 13% for synthetic task graphs in comparison with the in-phase schedules.
